Matthew Walker
Analyst, Credit Suisse
Thanks a lot. Hi, Mark. Hi, Jo. The first question is on tech. Obviously, you don't have a crystal ball, the tech actual advertising numbers are getting better in terms of their revenues. When do you think that they will start marketing again? Is it related to product innovation, or is it going to be related to their revenue growth? Could we see some in H2 2023, or do you think it's more likely that they rebound from a marketing point of view in 2024? Second question was, you mentioned margin and staff utilization hopefully getting better. Do you have something like Marcel which can increase utilization? Are you working on anything like that or what is the sort of WPP solution to utilization? The final question was on the property.
Are you going to increase the GBP 600 million savings target as a result of the charges taken against property?
Mark Read
CEO, WPP
Okay. If I tackle technology clients, as you say, I don't have a crystal ball. I do think that we're sort of at a unique point where growth has slowed. The companies have driven their share price by rebuilding margins, and we're at a point in the innovation cycle where there's an article in "The FT" today that talks about the number of new products being launched, but technology companies are not entirely clear on what the business model is associated with that. That very much bears in line the conversations I've had with these companies around their product innovation. I would expect that to revert, but I think that we're rightly being cautious about the likelihood of that happening in the course of this year, and that's reflected in perhaps the range of the guidance.
If you think about our guidance on a H2 basis, it's sort of 1% to 4% in the H2, and that's reflected in that range. These clients haven't totally stopped spending. It's really that they pulled back. I don't think that that will continue forever. On the topic of Marcel and staff allocation, we do have systems in each of our businesses that help us identify staff. We are using AI to pull staff from our systems to put on projects. Actually, it's interesting, Satalia, the AI company we use, is used by one of the big four accounting service firms to allocate their staff to projects and we have had a lot of success.
You'll see some of the success we've had in reducing our freelance cost by better utilizing staff across the business, both within our agencies and across our agencies. That is something that I think that we will continue to implement. Joanne, do you want to take the.
Joanne Wilson
CFO, WPP
Yep. Yeah. Hi, Matthew. Just on the property savings. This year, certainly underpins the GBP 450, which gives us confidence we'll deliver at least the GBP 450 this year. Looking at real estate as a whole, there are other areas of inflation. Energy is higher. As we open campuses, we see higher facilities costs associated with that. All of that savings this year, which we estimate to be around GBP 30 million, doesn't necessarily flow to the bottom line. In terms of the GBP 600, the way I think you should consider it is it accelerates us towards the GBP 600 rather than we'll now overlay the GBP 600 and say the GBP 600 is a bigger number. Certainly, it will help us accelerate to that target.
Matthew Walker
Analyst, Credit Suisse
Okay. Thanks a lot.

Tom Singlehurst
Analyst, Citi
Yeah. Good morning. It's Tom here from Citi. Thank you for taking the question. I've got two broad questions, although the first one is a two-parter, so I will just warn you on that.
Mark Read
CEO, WPP
That sounds like four, Tom.
Tom Singlehurst
Analyst, Citi
Yeah. Exactly. It's three questions, really. First group of questions. If we characterize it as being spend that is quasi CapEx that's being delayed and spend that is cost of goods sold that's continuing, I think that's possibly the way we interpret GroupM chunking along at six and some of the project-based work coming under pressure. I suppose the first question is, are you more exposed to CapEx style work in the US and COGS-like work internationally? Is there a sort of structural exposure issue that explains the growth differential, or do you think it's macro? That was the first question. The second one is linked to that. When you speak to your fellow CEOs, what is the factor that they're looking for to help get the confidence to turn the CapEx style spend back on? Those are the first two questions.
The third one is, you're guiding to 1.5% to 3%, which is for H2, 1% to 4%. Given what's happening in the rest of the world, and that's quite robust and possibly gets better, are you really just saying that the US could be anywhere between -5% and +1% in H2? Is all of that variance the US, essentially? Thank you.
Mark Read
CEO, WPP
I don't even know where to begin, Tom. I think the answer to your first question, I think that's a good way of thinking about it in terms of a quasi-CapEx and farther cost of goods sold, and it kind of explains why GroupM has continued to grow. I think the reason the impact is in the US and in our integrated creative agencies is more to do with where those clients spend most money and where we do most work for them. Also we happen to be probably stronger in our creative agencies, and we do some media for those technology companies, but not media for all of those technology companies. It's really a question of where the balance of work has fallen. I think if I talk about client confidence, I was at a CEO event earlier this week.
I think that confidence is not bad, but not good. I think it's probably pretty much where it was 3 months ago. You'll have seen your peer, Goldman, reduce their recession risk. I think there's a sense that US inflation is a little bit back under control, but some nervousness instead is lingering about consumer spending. I think we're really trying to evaluate what would happen to technology spend and technology-related projects and how clients will start to reinvest in the more, as you call it, CapEx-intensive parts of the business. I'll let Joanne talk to the guidance for consistency.
Joanne Wilson
CFO, WPP
Yeah. Tom, if you think about 1% to 4% in H2, maybe let me start at the bottom end of that. In Q2, we saw our like-for-like drop to 1.3%. As we roll forward, what are we seeing today? I think we'd say things feel like they're stabilizing. They're not getting any worse, they're not getting any better. If that like-for-like performance continued through H2, with a little bit more caution, would that be about 1%? That's really how we think about that bottom end, albeit we do have softer comps in H2, so it does assume a further deterioration, and it's probably a cautious bottom end of our range, as you'd expect. In terms of the top end, the 4%, that reflects really the softer comps that we see in H2.
If you look at last year, in H1 we grew at 0.9%, in H2 we grew 5.1%, so that should be a tailwind in H2. We have visibility over new business, some new business that we won only at 2022 that's ramping up, and we'll start to see more of a benefit from that as we go through the back half of Q3 and into Q4. Also some more recent new business wins from the last four to six weeks that we will ramp up again sort of in that time period, so the end of Q3 and through Q4. Good visibility on that. I think what is unknown, of course, is what stops. In the tech space in Q2, we haven't lost clients. It's clients choosing to either reduce spend or delay projects across mostly ECT.
What happens to that in H2? That's really the unknown. Of course, as Mark talked of in the macro, it's still very uncertain. Business doesn't like that. That's really resulting in the caution that we're seeing across our client base, which our peers have talked about as well. That's really how we're thinking about the 1% to 4% in H2.
Tom Singlehurst
Analyst, Citi
Very clear. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. We have no further questions, so I'd like to hand back the call to Mr Mark Read for further closing remarks.
Mark Read
CEO, WPP
Well, thank you very much, everybody, for listening. As you can see, we had a mixed H1 of the year, but I think we should take some comfort from the performance outside the United States. No doubt the United States was impacted, as we talked about, by the impact of technology companies. I think we should be pleased as well with the disciplined cost control and the improvement we made in the margin on a like-for-like basis in the H1 of the year. We'll continue to focus on those elements in the rest of the year. Thank you, everybody, for joining us.
